trick: Colligative means it counts particles and ignores what they are — so one mole of glucose and one mole of NaCl do not give the same effect, because NaCl gives two particles. That factor is the van't Hoff i, and forgetting it is the standard slip. Relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure are the four, and all four move with the number of solute particles.

data.prompt: Work out a freezing point depression, watching the van't Hoff factor.
data.problem: 0.1 mol of NaCl is dissolved in 1 kg of water. Kf for water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Assume complete dissociation.

steps.ask: What is the molality of the solution?
steps.why: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent: 0.1 mol in 1 kg is 0.1 m.

steps.ask: What is the van't Hoff factor for NaCl on complete dissociation?
steps.why: NaCl gives Na⁺ and Cl⁻ — two particles per formula unit.

steps.ask: At what temperature does the solution freeze?
steps.why: The freezing point is depressed below 0 °C, so it is −0.372 °C. Depression always lowers, elevation always raises.

data.answer: ΔTf = 0.372 K, so the solution freezes at −0.372 °C. Glucose at the same molality would give only half as much, because i = 1.

trick: Adsorption is at the surface, absorption is throughout the bulk — 'ad' means at. In colloids, learn the pair of names for each system: sol is solid in liquid, gel is liquid in solid, emulsion is liquid in liquid, aerosol is liquid or solid in gas. Note that milk, blood, cheese and paint are ALL colloids, so a question asking for 'the colloid' among them has no single answer.

trick: Count the lone pairs before naming the shape. Four electron pairs around the central atom always give a tetrahedral ARRANGEMENT, but the SHAPE is what the atoms make: no lone pair is tetrahedral (CH₄), one lone pair is trigonal pyramidal (NH₃), two lone pairs is bent (H₂O). The exam wants the precise term — 'trigonal pyramidal', not just 'pyramidal'.

trick: Down a group, the inert pair effect makes the lower oxidation state more stable — which is why Pb(II) beats Pb(IV) and Bi(III) beats Bi(V). Across a period, non-metallic character rises. Almost every anomalous-property question in this chapter is one of those two trends being applied.

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about the p-block.

items.statement: The +3 state of thallium is more stable than the +1 state.
items.why: It is the other way round. The inert pair effect makes the lower state more stable as you go down group 13, so Tl(I) is the stable one.

items.statement: Nitrogen cannot expand its octet, but phosphorus can.
items.why: Nitrogen has no d orbitals available in its valence shell, which is why NCl₅ does not exist while PCl₅ does.

items.statement: Fluorine has a lower electron affinity than chlorine.
items.why: An anomaly worth remembering: the fluorine atom is so small that the incoming electron feels strong repulsion, so chlorine tops the group.

items.statement: Ozone is a stronger oxidising agent than oxygen.
items.why: It readily gives up an atom of nascent oxygen, which is why it is used to disinfect water and to bleach.

items.statement: All noble gases are completely unreactive.
items.why: Xenon forms real compounds such as XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeO₃. The heavier noble gases have lower ionisation enthalpy.

trick: Grignard reagents are destroyed by anything with an acidic hydrogen — water, alcohol, even a trace of moisture — so the apparatus must be perfectly dry. Which alcohol you get depends on the carbonyl you attack: formaldehyde gives primary, any other aldehyde gives secondary, and a ketone gives tertiary. That three-way rule answers most Grignard questions.

trick: The iodoform test does not detect 'alcohols' — it detects the CH₃–CH(OH)– group. So ethanol and propan-2-ol give the yellow precipitate, but methanol does not (no carbon beside it) and tertiary butanol does not (no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, and no methyl attached to it). If the alcohol has no methyl group next to the OH-bearing carbon, there is no iodoform however alcoholic it is.

trick: Tollen's and Fehling's separate aldehydes from ketones — but not always. In alkaline solution a ketone with an alpha-hydroxyl isomerises to an aldehyde, so fructose reduces Tollen's reagent even though it is a ketose. When a question asks how to distinguish glucose from fructose, the honest answer is bromine water, which oxidises only the true aldehyde.

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about carbonyl tests.

items.statement: Tollen's reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ordinary ketones.
items.why: The aldehyde is oxidised to the acid and Ag⁺ is reduced to silver metal. Simple ketones resist oxidation.

items.statement: Tollen's reagent can be used to tell glucose from fructose.
items.why: Both give a positive result. In the alkaline medium fructose isomerises to glucose and mannose, so it reduces Tollen's too — the classic exception.

items.statement: Bromine water distinguishes glucose from fructose.
items.why: Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent in neutral solution, so no isomerisation occurs. It oxidises the aldose glucose to gluconic acid and leaves fructose untouched.

items.statement: Fehling's solution works with aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde.
items.why: Aromatic aldehydes do not respond to Fehling's, though they do reduce Tollen's — a distinction worth holding on to.

items.statement: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols.
items.why: The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance over two equivalent oxygens; carboxylic acids liberate CO₂ from bicarbonate, phenols do not.

trick: Sort the sugars by two tests. Reducing or not: all monosaccharides reduce, and among the common disaccharides only sucrose does not, because both its reducing groups are locked in the glycosidic bond. Aldose or ketose: glucose is an aldose, fructose a ketose — but remember that in alkali fructose behaves like an aldose.

trick: Addition polymers keep every atom of the monomer and need a double bond; condensation polymers lose a small molecule, usually water, and need two functional groups. So polythene and PVC are addition, nylon and terylene are condensation — and a monomer with no double bond can never make an addition polymer.
